title: Public safety can be experienced without becoming police-visible
source_unit: Bureau of Justice Statistics National Crime Victimization Survey; 2024 legacy-instrument estimates

denominator.unit: persons age 12 or older for violent victimization; households for property victimization

violent_victimization_rate.unit: victimizations per 1,000 persons age 12 or older

violent_reported_to_police_rate.unit: reported violent victimizations per 1,000 persons age 12 or older

violent_share_reported.unit: percent of violent victimizations reported to police

property_share_reported.unit: percent of property victimizations reported to police

police_visibility_boundary.value: not all experienced victimization enters police records

observations.method: BJS analysis of the 2024 National Crime Victimization Survey legacy instrument; the survey asks about nonfatal victimizations reported and not reported to police and reasons for reporting status.
observations.uncertainty: The 2024 NCVS used a split sample while the redesigned instrument was phased in, so the report focuses on the legacy half-sample and notes lower precision. Survey estimates do not reconstruct every incident, measure police response quality, or follow victims through safety, remedy, trust, or later action.
observations.subgroup: Persons age 12 or older and sampled U.S. households; BJS reports variation by crime type and selected demographic and residence characteristics.
observations.counterinterpretation: Nonreporting can reflect fear, privacy, a belief that police could not help, a personal interpretation, or perceived triviality; it does not by itself prove distrust or institutional failure. A report does not prove a useful response or improved safety.

related_sources.claim: BJS publication page identifies the report, its scope, and the 2024 legacy/redesigned instrument split.
BJS distinguishes survey victimization estimates from law-enforcement-recorded NIBRS data.

boundary: This record adds a public-safety visibility boundary: experienced victimization, reporting, police records, response, victim services, safety, trust, and collective action are separate stages. It does not establish why a person did or did not report, whether police helped, whether safety improved, or whether victimization changed political behavior.
